title: U.S. Wholesale Prices Flat in July as Energy Costs Decline
excerpt: The Producer Price Index was unchanged in July, coming in below expectations as falling fuel costs offset rising services prices, signaling potential relief for consumers.
body:
• The Producer Price Index was unchanged in July, below the 0.1% monthly increase economists had forecast
  • Year-over-year wholesale inflation slowed to 4.7% from 5.5% in June, the sharpest monthly deceleration in 2026
  • Energy costs fell 3.1% month over month, with gasoline prices down 5.7%, driving most of the cooldown
  • Core PPI rose 0.2% for the month, cooling to 4.2% annually — the lowest in four months
  • The data lowers the odds of a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike in September

Wholesale Inflation Comes in Cooler Than Expected

U.S. wholesale prices were flat in July, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday, delivering a reading that came in softer than the 0.1% monthly increase economists had anticipated. On a year-over-year basis, the Producer Price Index rose 4.7%, a meaningful pullback from June's 5.5% pace, according to BLS data.

The cooler reading signals that businesses are seeing some relief from the sharp price increases that dominated earlier in 2026 and could portend easing consumer inflation in the months ahead.

"Most input costs beyond energy are cooling. That should reduce inflationary pressures for businesses in coming months."

— Ben Ayers, Senior Economist, Nationwide

Energy Prices Drive the Decline

Falling fuel costs were the primary force behind the flat reading. Energy costs dropped 3.1% month over month, with gasoline prices tumbling 5.7%, according to Barron's. More than half of the July decrease in the index for final demand goods was driven by the pullback in gasoline costs alone.

Food prices also continued their decline, falling 0.9% on the month. Combined, the index for final demand goods dropped 0.7% in July, according to the BLS data.

Wholesale inflation had climbed to a four-year high of 5.9% in May after geopolitical tensions caused a spike in oil and gas prices, according to CNN. The June and July readings suggest that surge is now unwinding.

Services Costs and the AI Factor

While goods prices retreated, services costs rose 0.2% in July, driven largely by portfolio management fees, which jumped 6.5%, according to Barron's. In contrast, truck freight prices fell 1.8% and airfares declined 3.4%, indicating the earlier oil-price spike has not produced broad-based inflationary pressure.

The data also revealed the ongoing impact of artificial intelligence investment on producer costs. Semiconductor and electronic component manufacturing prices were up 27.1% year over year, while computer hardware and software retailing costs surged 11.9% in a single month, according to Barron's — reflecting how the AI build-out is creating localized price pressures even as broader inflation cools.

What It Means for the Fed

Core PPI, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.2% in July — a pullback from June's revised 0.4% increase. On an annual basis, core producer prices climbed 4.2%, down from 4.7% in June, marking the lowest rate in four months.

Citi economists now estimate that core PCE — the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge — will increase 0.2% month over month for July, putting the 12-month rate at 3.2%, according to Barron's. The Bureau of Economic Analysis will release the July PCE data on August 26.

The softer wholesale inflation numbers lower the likelihood of a Fed interest-rate increase in September, though fuel prices remain a wild card given ongoing geopolitical conflicts, analysts noted.

What's Next

Thursday's PPI data arrives one day after the Consumer Price Index showed that consumer inflation cooled for the second straight month to an annual rate of 3.4%, according to CNN. Together, the readings paint a picture of gradually moderating price pressures heading into fall.

However, prices are still rising considerably faster than their pre-2020 pace, and the compounding effect of five-plus years of elevated inflation continues to strain household budgets. The Fed's next policy meeting in September will be a key test of whether the central bank views the recent trend as sufficient to hold rates steady.
nri_angle: Cooling wholesale inflation could ease price pressures for American workers and consumers, including Indian-American households navigating elevated living costs.
